analysis.investment_thesis: MedPlus is a structurally sound pharma retailer riding India's healthcare formalization wave, but at 10,544 Cr market cap and 50.9x P/E with sub-9% ROE, it fails every SMILE valuation and size criterion. There is no margin of safety here — this is an institutional story, not a multibagger discovery.
key_strengths: Revenue CAGR 15.1% and operating income CAGR 33.2% over 9 years shows meaningful operational leverage kicking in
FY25 FCF surged to 482 Cr (from 61 Cr in FY24) — capital intensity is easing as store network matures
Large underpenetrated Indian pharma retail TAM with diagnostic services and private-label creating vertical integration
key_risks: Market cap of 10,544 Cr is 5-10x outside the SMILE sweet spot — institutional ownership (FII 16.83% + DII 26.58%) means no information asymmetry edge
P/E of 50.9x on razor-thin 4.75% operating margins leaves zero room for error — a margin slip sends the stock crashing
Borrowings rising steadily from 477 Cr (2020) to 1,193 Cr (2025) with D/E at 0.65, above the 0.4 comfort level
red_flags: Promoter holding of 40.29% is well below the 50% minimum — no strong skin-in-the-game signal
ROE of 8.8% and ROCE of 10.3% are deeply inadequate for a 50x P/E stock — capital is not being deployed efficiently
Net profit trajectory is erratic: 9→29→42→12→2→63→95→50→66→150 Cr — volatile and undependable
analysis.detailed_analysis:
MedPlus fails the SMILE framework at almost every checkpoint. At 10,544 Cr market cap, it is already widely discovered — FIIs and DIIs together own 43%+ of the float, meaning the easy re-rating from obscurity to visibility has long passed. The business is fundamentally a thin-margin retail operation: 25.86% gross margins compress to just 4.75% operating margins after store costs, leaving net profit of only 150 Cr on 6,136 Cr of revenues — a net margin barely above 2.4%. A P/E of 50.9x on these economics is pricing in perfection across a decade of execution. Kedia's framework demands 8–15x P/E entries precisely to protect against this kind of downside compression.

The one genuinely interesting data point is FY25's FCF explosion to 482 Cr — driven by OCF of 540 Cr and capex falling to just 59 Cr — suggesting the store rollout phase is maturing and the network is beginning to harvest cash. But even this is insufficient justification at current prices. ROE of 8.8% signals that the business generates poor returns on the equity raised (it did a large equity raise in FY22, inflating the denominator). Promoter holding at 40.29% and rising debt (D/E 0.65) are additional disqualifiers. This is a decent business for a long-only fund at a fair price — not a Kedia-style multibagger at this valuation.
